fatal_errors: The proposed elevated-temperature, constant-load experiment does not match the room-temperature nanoindentation-creep regime of the target study.
It omits modulation-period control and therefore cannot recover the non-monotonic optimum at 16 nm or distinguish coherent, semicoherent, and grain-boundary-dominated multilayers.

The mechanism incorrectly treats suppression of dislocation glide and climb as the complete explanation, missing the proposed transition at semicoherent interfaces to diffusion or interface-slip creep associated with localized stress and possible interfacial amorphization.
The cited studies concern bulk HEAs and do not support multilayer-interface pinning, interface coherency, or the claimed coating-creep comparison.
explanation: The hypothesis captures only the broad idea that multilayer interfaces impede dislocations and may reduce creep. It does not reconstruct the decisive variable—layer modulation period—or the specific comparison among 8, 16, 32, and 80 nm coatings. Its monolithic baseline is a reasonable generic control, but it cannot reveal why the semicoherent 16 nm architecture outperforms both coherent-interface and grain-boundary-dominated coatings. The conditions and stated applicability are substantially mismatched: the target concerns room-temperature, 5 mN nanoindentation creep, whereas the generated proposal concerns elevated-temperature macroscopic creep and time to failure. The experiment could test whether multilayers outperform monolithic material, but would not establish interface coherency as the governing mediator without systematically varying period and measuring interface structure, stress exponents, and post-deformation interfacial changes. The falsification rule addresses overall performance rather than whether dislocation pinning is dominant, since equal or lower creep alone cannot distinguish pinning from diffusion, interface slip, residual stress, grain-size effects, or compositional strengthening.
